problem: Existing EQA pipelines follow a store-then-retrieve paradigm built for temporally stable scenes; in human-populated dynamic scenes, occlusions and human activity make cues transient and view-dependent. Such pipelines commit ambiguous single views to memory and over-accumulate redundant evidence, which raises inference cost.
motivation: Real-world EQA agents must be robust to human motion and occlusion while staying efficient. Structured alternatives such as 3D scene graphs reduce duplication but carry heavy perception and maintenance overhead. The authors observe that a single relevance signal can drive both verifying ambiguous views and deciding what to store.
key_idea: Use a VLM-derived question-conditioned relevance score to trigger in-place multi-view rotation that verifies ambiguous observations, and to gate admission so that only verified, highly relevant views enter a compact memory.
insight: Selecting the best view before memory commitment improves evidence fidelity without growing memory, because the intermediate views are discarded. In the ablation, adding Adaptive Memory to the FBE baseline gives 46.3→51.9, View Refinement gives 53.5, and Room Detection gives 56.6 with less memory (9.5 vs 10.3). Global coverage (frontier exploration) and local view disambiguation are complementary: RE and GOE reach only 33.9 and 36.3, while FBE+VR reaches 56.6. Prior memory-heavy baselines degrade in dynamic scenes: MemoryEQA gets 29.8 on Dynamic with 73.6 memory entries.
method: Target-Region Reasoning: a VLM is prompted with (observation, question); the softmax over Yes-token logits among candidate polar tokens (τ=1) gives a relevance score s_t∈[0,1]. An optional region likelihood ρ_t gates refinement.
View Refinement trigger: refinement is activated when τ_rot ≤ s_t < τ_mem (an ambiguity band, 0.6 to 0.8), and also ρ_t ≥ τ_reg if region gating is on.
Multi-view augmentation: the agent rotates in place to collect at most K≤3 extra views (FOV 110°), re-scores each view, and takes the argmax-relevance view as the verified view.
Relevance-driven Memory Admission: the verified view is written to memory at most once per waypoint, only if s ≥ τ_mem=0.8 and it passes a lightweight image-quality Valid() filter.
Compact memory entry: each entry stores the CLIP ViT-L/14 embedding (768-D), the agent pose and the image.
Action and answer: the policy A_t=π(O_t,Q,M_t) is built on the Explore-EQA frontier-based exploration backbone, and the VLM answers from Q and the final compact memory.
DynHiL-EQA dataset: Habitat/MP3D, 1,100 VLM-generated multi-view QA pairs in 7 categories, split into 550 Dynamic (injected human motion) and 550 Static questions.

setting.observation: egocentric RGB (with pose), rotated views at 110° FOV
setting.action_space: frontier-based exploration waypoints (Explore-EQA style) plus in-place rotations

numbers.extra: training-free; FOV 110°, up to 3 auxiliary views

numbers_note: The paper gives no explicit split names for its benchmarks; 'test' and 'val' were assigned by convention. Times were converted to seconds as printed.
results: On DynHiL-EQA, DIVRR reaches 56.6% overall and 55.1% on the Dynamic split, a 7.4-point gain overall and 10.1 points on Dynamic over the strongest baseline. Graph-EQA scores 49.2 overall and Fine-EQA 45.0 on Dynamic. Dynamic-split memory is cut by 74% relative to Graph-EQA, at ~5.7 s latency. On HM-EQA it reaches 63.8% vs 60.4% for Graph-EQA, with 2.51 memory entries vs 6.04.
limitations: No explicit temporal consistency in evidence validation, so failures occur when transient cues evolve over multiple timesteps.
Open-world object changes and complex socially-aware human behaviors can invalidate earlier observations.
The dataset is small (1,100 questions) and VLM-generated; relevance thresholds (0.6/0.8) are hand-set, and evaluation uses only a 7B VLM with a few baselines.
